newsitem.title: NORWAY: Iceland volcano eruption fades but floods expected.
newsitem.headline: Iceland volcano eruption fades but floods expected.

text.p: Scientists said on Monday a volcanic eruption under a giant glacier on Iceland's southeast coast appeared to be dying out, but emergency services remained on full alert for massive flooding from the melted ice.

The volcano under the Vatnajokull glacier has been spewing ash and steam since September 30 and has melted large parts of the ice cap, causing tonnes of water to accumulate in the nearby Grimsvotn subglacial lake.
The water is threatening to break through the ice and flood down to the vast, uninhabitated black sand plains at the foot of the isolated glacier.
Seismologists at the University of Iceland have been continually monitoring the earth tremors caused by the eruption to see its strength.
"We have seen a decrease in eruption vigour. I can barely detect the eruption tremor now," seismologist Bryndis Brandsdottir told Reuters in a telephone interview.
"It appears the eruption is dying or may already be dead."
Icelandic television journalist Omar Ragnarsson said the decline in the power of eruption was clearly visible during a flight over the volcano on Sunday.

"In the morning the (eruption) column was up to about 9,000 feet (2,750 metres) but it was much smaller later in the day. Normally black ash spews out of the fissure at intervals but there was no ash yesterday, just rising vapour," Ragnarsson said.
Since the eruption began, Iceland has been preparing for a torrent of water, ice and debris to be released when the icecap eventually gives way under the strain of Grimsvotn's rising water levels.

The black sand plain surrounding the desolate glacier, located about 250 km (150 miles) east of Reykjavik, is uninhabitated but government workers have been toiling to protect the country's one coastal ring road and bridges and power and telecommunication lines passing through the area.

Leading geophysicist Magnus Tumi Gudmundsson said the rate at which the melted water was rising had slowed considerably as the eruption faded and because of a widening of the lake's basin near the top.

At the weekend scientists measured the height of Grimsvotn's water level at 1,500 metres (4,921 ft) above sea level, indicating that about 3 trillion litres (660 billion gallons) of water had collected there.
Gudmundsson said that despite the slowdown there was no doubt the floods would come.

"We think the lake may be rising about one metre (3.3 feet) a day but that's rather uncertain. But the lake is 45 metres (148 ft) above the highest previously recorded level at which it has flooded before," he said.
"This is a highly unusual and unstable situation. It could be hours, it could be days or it could just as well be weeks, but the flood will come."
